title: Vaccine Mandates
scope: Requiring vaccination as a condition of school, work or public life, and standing emergency powers for the next pandemic.

overview.summary: Requiring vaccination for school or work: which shots, whose consent, and who decides where public health power ends.
overview.scope_covered: Vaccination required for school, work, or public access: legal authority, which diseases qualify, exemption design, enforcement, and effects on uptake and trust.
overview.scope_excluded: The underlying safety and efficacy science, approval and liability regimes, lockdowns and masking, and global supply and access equity.
overview.why_now: Kindergarten vaccine exemptions reached a record 4.2% in CDC data released on August 17, 2026, as federal officials rewrite the childhood schedule and states move in opposite directions.

stats.label: Coverage needed to stop measles spreading · two-dose MMR
stats.note: One measles case can seed 12 to 18 more, so spread stops reliably only once coverage clears about 95 percent.
stats.detail: The reproduction number behind that threshold, 12 to 18 secondary cases per infection, is among the highest of any human pathogen, and because unvaccinated families cluster by school and neighborhood rather than mixing randomly through the population, a national average above the line can still leave individual communities well below it. It is the benchmark every coverage figure in this topic gets measured against, and one of the only numbers every position accepts as settled science even while disagreeing sharply on how a population should reach it.

stats.label: Kindergarten MMR coverage · national average
stats.note: Two-dose measles coverage among kindergartners has slipped below the roughly 95 percent needed to stop outbreaks.
stats.detail: CDC’s 2025 to 2026 school-year data put kindergarten coverage at 92.4 percent for MMR, 92.0 percent for DTaP and 92.4 percent for polio, down from about 95 percent for all three in the last pre-pandemic year, 2019 to 2020. The national figure hides wide state variation: several states still report coverage above 95 percent while others sit well under 90 percent, which is why the coverage question turns as much on geography and local clustering as on the nationwide number.

stats.label: Kindergartners exempted from a vaccine · national rate
stats.note: About one in 24 kindergartners now starts school exempt from at least one required vaccine, up from 2.5 percent before the pandemic and the highest rate CDC has recorded.
stats.detail: Of the 4.2 percent exemption rate for 2025 to 2026, roughly 4.0 percentage points are non-medical (religious or philosophical) exemptions rather than medical ones, up from 2.5 percent overall before the pandemic (2019 to 2020). Exemptions rose in most states that report them. Whether the rise reflects more parents refusing outright, easier exemption paperwork, or families shifting to homeschooling and private school instead of complying is itself one of this topic’s open empirical questions.

stats.label: US measles cases in 2025 · worst year in three decades
stats.note: Cases cluster in unvaccinated communities rather than spreading evenly, and 2026 has already run higher than 2025.
stats.detail: Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, meaning no strain circulated continuously for 12 months. Health authorities describe the country as highly likely to lose that status when it is formally reassessed in November 2026, if the ongoing chain of transmission is confirmed to trace to a single imported strain running longer than 12 months. That the cases sit in a handful of under-vaccinated communities rather than spread evenly is why they are read so differently: one camp sees proof that the exemption door is too wide, another sees proof that outreach never reached those communities.
stats.source_label: CIDRAP, US highly likely to lose measles elimination status this fall

stats.label: Year the Supreme Court upheld mandate power · Jacobson v. Massachusetts
stats.note: Jacobson v. Massachusetts held that a state may compel vaccination over an individual’s objection, the legal foundation under every mandate since.
stats.detail: The 7-2 ruling upheld a Massachusetts town’s smallpox vaccination order, holding that “the liberty secured by the Constitution... does not import an absolute right in each person to be... freed from restraint” when the community faces an epidemic disease. It supplies the constitutional floor under every state school and workplace vaccine requirement discussed in this topic, but it has never been read to require any particular exemption design, leaving that choice entirely to state legislatures.
stats.source_label: Jacobson v. Massachusetts, 197 U.S. 11, Cornell Legal Information Institute

stats.label: Coverage change after ending non-medical exemptions · California
stats.note: After California eliminated religious and personal-belief exemptions in 2016, kindergartners fully vaccinated for school rose from 92.8 percent to 95.1 percent in two years, while medical exemptions more than tripled.
stats.detail: Medical exemptions went from 0.2 percent to 0.7 percent of kindergartners over the same period, as some families found physicians willing to grant them under the law’s broader medical standard. The net effect was still a substantial coverage gain, the case study most often cited by anyone weighing a similar law elsewhere, though it also shows that closing the non-medical exemption door alone does not close every path around a mandate.
stats.source_label: Pediatrics, Elimination of Nonmedical Immunization Exemptions in California and School-Entry Vaccine Status

stats.label: States allowing a religious or philosophical exemption · out of 50
stats.note: All 50 states require core vaccines for school entry and all 50 plus DC allow a medical exemption; only 45 plus DC add a religious or philosophical one.
stats.detail: There is no federal school-vaccine mandate: the 10th Amendment leaves the requirements, and the exemption design, entirely to the states, consistent with Jacobson. Five states (California, Connecticut, Maine, New York and West Virginia, the last contested in court as of August 2026) allow only a medical exemption; the other 45 plus DC add a religious exemption, a philosophical one, or both, with the paperwork required ranging from a signed form to a notarized affidavit. This is the structural reason the topic’s “who decides” question has dozens of different answers rather than one.
stats.source_label: KFF, state and local policies on school vaccine requirements

stats.label: Vote blocking the federal workplace mandate · Supreme Court
stats.note: In NFIB v. OSHA (2022), the Supreme Court blocked a federal vaccine-or-test rule for employers with 100 or more workers, ruling OSHA lacked authority for a general public-health measure.
stats.detail: The blocked rule would have covered roughly 84 million workers. The majority held that workplace-safety law does not extend to regulating the public at large just because people happen to hold a job, drawing a sharp line between the federal government’s narrow workplace-safety authority and the states’ broader police power affirmed in Jacobson. It is why workplace vaccine mandates in this topic are overwhelmingly a state, employer or industry-licensing matter rather than a federal one; a companion ruling issued the same day, Biden v. Missouri, upheld a narrower requirement for workers at Medicare- and Medicaid-funded health care facilities by 5-4.
stats.source_label: Oyez, National Federation of Independent Business v. Department of Labor

stats.label: States no longer following federal vaccine guidance · out of 50
stats.note: By August 2026, 27 states had said they will no longer comprehensively follow CDC and its outside vaccine advisory committee on the childhood schedule, up from 9 in September 2025.
stats.detail: Three more states have delinked for specific vaccines only (Alaska and Mississippi for hepatitis B, Arizona for hepatitis B and COVID-19), bringing the total departing in some form to 28 jurisdictions including DC. The split followed changes to the membership and recommendations of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) in 2025 and 2026, and it means the “who decides” question in this topic no longer has a single federal answer to react to: state legislatures, medical boards and professional bodies (the American Academy of Pediatrics now issues its own schedule) are increasingly setting policy independently of each other and of Washington.
stats.source_label: KFF, state recommendations for routine childhood vaccines

stats.label: Coverage under a medical-only exemption policy · Mississippi & West Virginia
stats.note: For over three decades Mississippi and West Virginia were the only states barring every non-medical exemption, and both have topped the national coverage table; West Virginia still leads at 98.9 percent.
stats.detail: The comparison is no longer clean at either end. Mississippi’s ban fell first, when a federal court in Bosarge v. Edney ordered the state to start granting religious exemptions from July 15, 2023. West Virginia’s governor then issued an executive order in January 2025 reopening religious and philosophical exemptions, on hold and unenforced pending a ruling from the state Supreme Court. Today Mississippi grants religious exemptions under a federal court order, while West Virginia remains medical-only by statute.

questions.text: Do school and workplace requirements actually raise vaccination coverage, or mainly push refusers into exemptions, homeschooling, and private schools?
questions.why: Proponents call school-entry rules the one lever tied to durable high coverage; critics say determined refusers simply route around them, so the headline number hides substitution rather than persuasion.
questions.detail:
School-entry laws with narrow exemptions are the policy most consistently linked to coverage near the threshold needed for herd protection, because they make vaccination the default most parents simply comply with rather than fight. States that tightened exemption pathways, closing personal-belief exemptions in particular, saw coverage recover, which the Guardian position reads as proof the lever still works once the loophole around it is closed.

The Schedule Minimalist and Medical Freedom camps counter that school-reported coverage obscures where the unvaccinated child actually went. A family blocked by a strict entry rule doesn’t necessarily vaccinate; it may claim a religious exemption, move to a private or charter school with laxer enforcement, or homeschool outright, so the child leaves the ledger without ever getting the shot. Where exemption paperwork is easy, opt-out rates track the friction of the process more than genuine belief, meaning mandates may be measuring compliance with a form rather than a change in behavior.

questions.text: Where does a person’s claim over their own body yield to protecting those who cannot be protected any other way?
questions.why: The topic’s foundational rights clash: bodily autonomy against what is owed to infants and the immunocompromised, who cannot be vaccinated and depend entirely on everyone else’s immunity.
questions.detail:
The Guardian and Confidence Builder positions both start from the premise that autonomy has never been treated as absolute in law: when refusal creates a foreseeable physical risk to a third party who has no way to protect themselves, the classroom or workplace is a shared space, not private property, and entering it while contagious-risk is elevated looks closer to endangerment than personal choice. That reasoning is why courts have historically upheld compulsory vaccination as a public-safety power rather than a private medical decision.

The Medical Freedom and Conscience Broadener camps read the same facts oppositely: consent to any intervention carrying risk is a right that cannot be overridden by someone else’s hypothetical benefit, and “protecting the vulnerable” has licensed state overreach before without the actual risk calculus getting a real hearing. They place the line much further out, reserving compulsion for only the most severe, classroom-transmissible diseases and treating every case short of that as the state substituting its judgment for the individual’s.

questions.text: What must a disease and its vaccine demonstrate before compulsion is justified at all?
questions.why: Every camp accepts that some threshold must exist before the state can compel a shot; they split sharply on how high to set it and which diseases clear it.
questions.detail:
The Herd Immunity Guardian sets the bar at severe harm plus ready transmission in shared spaces, which puts measles squarely inside mandate territory: a single unvaccinated case in a classroom can seed an outbreak that reaches infants and the immunocompromised nearby, and the vaccine’s record of driving such diseases toward elimination is the demonstrated payoff that is held to justify the intrusion.

The Schedule Minimalist insists severity and classroom transmissibility must both be present, not either alone, which is why they would strike hepatitis B (bloodborne, not casually spread among schoolchildren) and chickenpox (mild in most cases) from the entry list while keeping measles and polio on it. The Medical Freedom Campaigner rejects the premise altogether: severity and transmissibility explain why vaccination is advisable, in this reading, never why it may be forced.

questions.text: Who holds the authority to decide: federal agencies, state legislatures, school boards, physicians, or parents?
questions.why: Authority here is genuinely split across five levels, and each camp favors whichever body is likeliest to rule its way, so the jurisdictional question doubles as a proxy fight.
questions.detail:
States hold the core police power over public health, which is why school-entry law varies so much between them; federal agencies mainly set a recommended schedule that states then choose whether to enforce. The Guardian position wants that authority to stay with public-health bodies insulated from electoral swings, on the logic that epidemiology, not a legislative session, should set the bar for a classroom-wide risk.

The Conscience Broadener and Medical Freedom camps push the decision down toward the individual: a school board or state legislature answers to a political majority, not to the specific family bearing the medical risk, so final say over an intervention performed on one’s own body belongs with the parent or treating physician. Where authority should sit therefore tracks a deeper value split, trust in expert bodies against trust in individual conscience, more than it tracks any settled reading of the law.

questions.text: Does compulsion erode public trust enough that voluntary uptake later falls further than it first rose?
questions.why: Forcing compliance now may cost more in later voluntary uptake than it buys immediately, an effect that plays out over years against a shifting political climate and is correspondingly hard to isolate.
questions.detail:
The Confidence Builder position points to the backlash pattern that follows aggressive mandates: hardened distrust, mobilized anti-mandate politics, and exemption rates that ratchet upward each time the schedule expands. Coercion, on this account, trades a short compliance bump for a longer erosion of the voluntary goodwill public health depends on once the mandate can’t reach a population, adults, unregulated workplaces, private settings.

The Herd Immunity Guardian and the mainstream public-health view read the correlation the other way: distrust was already rising for reasons unrelated to mandates, misinformation, polarization, high-profile safety scares, and mandates are the reason coverage held up as well as it did through that period. Without the requirement, on this view, uptake would have fallen further still, since the trust decline was happening regardless of policy.

questions.text: Should an exemption turn on the sincerity of a belief, and can any government test sincerity fairly?
questions.why: Without a sincerity test a religious or philosophical exemption can swallow the mandate; with one, the state ends up interrogating private conscience.
questions.detail:
The Conscience Exemption Broadener argues sincerity cannot be fairly adjudicated by a clerk or judge without turning the state into an arbiter of belief, an intrusion at least as troubling as the mandate itself. The safer rule, on this account, is to accept a stated belief at face value and treat some share of insincere claims as the acceptable cost of protecting the genuine ones.

The Herd Immunity Guardian points to states where religious-exemption rates rose sharply once personal-belief exemptions were closed, evidence read as proof that a no-questions-asked policy just relabels convenience-refusal as conviction. That pattern is part of why several states removed non-medical exemptions altogether rather than try to police sincerity, treating the whole sincerity-test project as unworkable in either direction rather than choosing a fairer version of it. Navin and Diekema’s answer is neither: don’t take the claim at face value, and don’t erase it either — require a counseling visit or education module before the waiver is granted, and let the friction itself do the sorting.

questions.text: How much of the recent coverage decline reflects refusal rather than cost, insurance churn, and disrupted clinic access?
questions.why: Crediting the whole slide in kindergarten coverage to refusal ignores the access side: lost insurance, missed appointments and pandemic gaps in care depress uptake among willing parents too.
questions.detail:
The Vaccine Confidence Builder stresses that a family that wants the vaccine but loses coverage, can’t get an appointment, or fell out of a well-child visit schedule shows up in the same “not fully vaccinated” statistic as a deliberate refuser. Treating the whole decline as a trust or belief problem risks prescribing exemption crackdowns for what is partly a logistics failure that outreach and access fixes, not enforcement, would actually solve.

The Herd Immunity Guardian points instead to exemption rates specifically, the category that isolates deliberate opt-out from access failure, which have also climbed over the same period. That is taken as evidence that refusal is a real and growing share of the decline, not merely an access story, since outreach alone hasn’t reversed the slide where exemption pathways stayed easy to use.

positions.name: Herd Immunity Guardian
positions.steelman: The only lever that ever held coverage at 95 percent: a doctor’s note or nothing.
positions.description: Herd immunity is not an abstraction: it is the only shield an infant too young for the MMR shot, or a child undergoing chemotherapy, will ever have. Measles is contagious enough that it takes roughly 95% two-dose coverage to stop transmission chains, and school-entry rules are the one lever that has actually held a population there. Let a philosophical or personal-belief box substitute for a doctor’s note and coverage drifts below that line, as it did across California for years; close that exit, as California’s SB277 did in 2016, and coverage moves back, with kindergartners fully vaccinated for school climbing from 92.8% to 95.1% within two years while personal-belief exemptions collapsed to under 0.01%. The price of a classroom seat is not surrendering conscience, it is not importing a disease that someone else’s child cannot survive.
positions.detail:
Every state already ties a set of vaccines to school enrollment; what varies is how easy the exit is, and this camp treats that exit as the whole fight. California, Connecticut, Maine, New York and West Virginia allow only a doctor’s signature; the other forty-five states plus DC still let a parent check a religious or philosophical box, and coverage in those states runs measurably lower and more exemption-clustered by school and zip code, the exact geography that turns one imported case into an outbreak. The American Academy of Pediatrics has pressed this point since 2016, reaffirming and updating its policy in Pediatrics in 2025 to call on every remaining state to eliminate all nonmedical exemptions as a condition of school attendance, advocating the elimination of nonmedical exemptions as contrary to optimal individual and public health.

The camp does not pretend the fix is costless or complete. In the Pediatrics study of SB277, over the two years after SB277 took effect, medical exemptions in California rose from 0.17 to 0.73 percent of kindergartners while personal-belief exemptions fell from 2.37 percent to under 0.01 percent, and homeschooling and independent-study enrollment, which the law left outside the requirement, absorbed some of the families who would otherwise have opted out; this camp reads that as containment working as designed, corralling a small population of genuine or borderline cases while the large majority of formerly exempted children got vaccinated, not as the policy failing. Where the argument sharpens is over which diseases belong on the list at all and how strictly ‘medical’ gets policed against a sympathetic doctor writing lenient notes; this camp holds the line at requiring the vaccine, not at accommodating a parent’s discomfort with it, and treats the residual fraction of a percent of nonmedical exemptions left standing as proof the model works rather than proof it has failed.
positions.proponents: Paul Offit, American Academy of Pediatrics, Richard Pan
positions.representative_note: Reaffirmed and updated its policy statement in 2025 calling on every remaining state to eliminate nonmedical exemptions from school vaccination requirements.

positions.name: Conscience Exemption Broadener
positions.steelman: Keep the mandate. No clerk gets to rule on whose faith is sincere enough to count.
positions.description: Nobody here disputes that a school or an employer may require a vaccine: measles and polio are real enough to justify a rule. What is disputed is a government’s claim to override a sincerely held religious or parental conviction once that rule meets resistance grounded in faith rather than convenience, because a conscience right that yields the moment it becomes inconvenient was never a right at all. Fairness shows up in administration, and the record is stark: figures cited in the Navy SEALs 1–26 litigation put Marine Corps approval of COVID vaccine religious exemption requests at 0.52% and the Navy’s at 1.02% while medical and administrative exemptions were granted routinely, an asymmetry federal courts read as a religious test in disguise and one that ended in a 2024 settlement clearing the records of thousands of sailors. A state that grants nearly every medical exemption and almost no religious one is not applying science more strictly, it is ranking one kind of conscience beneath another.
positions.detail:
Religious exemptions to school vaccination were once nearly universal: before 2015, forty-eight states allowed one, and only Mississippi and West Virginia did not. That consensus broke after the Disneyland measles outbreak, when California eliminated non-medical exemptions in 2015 and New York followed in 2019 amid outbreaks centered in Orthodox Jewish communities in Brooklyn and Rockland County. This camp reads those repeals not as proportionate public-health responses but as the moment several states decided a shot mandate could override the First Amendment’s free exercise clause outright, and it rests its case on a live shift in the underlying doctrine: Employment Division v. Smith (1990) let neutral, generally applicable laws skip religious exemptions entirely, but Fulton v. City of Philadelphia (2021) and Mahmoud v. Taylor (2025) have both narrowed that rule. How far it narrows is contested: on remand from the Supreme Court, the Second Circuit held in June 2026 that New York’s repeal was neutral and generally applicable and that Mahmoud did not disturb it, an outcome this camp reads as a lower court taking the trend too narrowly rather than as the end of the argument.

Approval-rate data made the case before argument did. Across the armed services’ COVID mandate, religious exemption approval rates ran as low as 0.52% (Marine Corps) and 1.02% (Navy), while medical and administrative exemptions were granted as a matter of course. That gap is what First Liberty Institute and Hacker Stephens LLP used to win a January 2022 injunction and then a 2024 settlement covering thousands of Navy servicemembers, which corrected their records and barred the next three promotion boards from considering the refusal. A parallel St. Louis case produced a jury verdict for teachers whose district approved the medical exemptions it received while denying religious requests, a ruling the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty backed on appeal. To this camp, a process that clears medical claims and rejects religious ones at these ratios is not screening for sincerity, it is screening out a category of belief.

Litigation lawyers and state legislators want different things here. Groups like Becket Fund and First Liberty Institute confine their argument to religious exercise, the narrower and more litigable claim under the First Amendment. Legislators go further: West Virginia’s SB 26 would add a philosophical and personal-conviction exemption alongside the religious one, and SB 237 would bar school vaccine mandates outright, which draws the sharper internal objection that an exemption open to any parent’s say-so risks becoming a loophole no state can police. For now the federal posture favors the broader reading: in September 2025, HHS’s Office for Civil Rights told every state administering the Vaccines for Children Program that it must honor state religious and conscience exemption laws, and West Virginia’s governor has pressed the same claim by executive order.
positions.proponents: First Liberty Institute, Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, Liberty Counsel, Gov. Patrick Morrisey (West Virginia)
positions.representative_note: Public-interest law firm that won the 2024 Navy SEALs 1-26 religious-exemption settlement with Hacker Stephens LLP; it argues for the exemption within the mandate, never against the mandate itself.

positions.name: Institutional Risk Owner
positions.steelman: Whoever answers for the harm sets the rule: the hospital, not the statehouse.
positions.description: A vaccination requirement is a risk decision, and it belongs to whoever answers for the harm: the hospital, the nursing home, the employer whose people share air with the vulnerable. Federal courts drew that line on January 13, 2022, blocking OSHA’s vaccinate-or-test rule for large employers as a general public-health measure beyond the agency’s remit and, the same day, upholding the CMS requirement for Medicare- and Medicaid-funded health care facilities, where infection control is the core of the job. That cuts against blanket state bans as hard as it cuts against blanket federal mandates: when Texas moved to forbid private employers from requiring COVID vaccination, the Texas Hospital Association opposed a blanket prohibition on hospital vaccine requirements and pushed for safeguards in the ban.
positions.detail:
The camp’s authority is professional rather than legislative. The American Hospital Association took the same line in July 2021, when its president said the AHA ‘supports hospitals and health systems that choose, based on local factors, to mandate COVID-19 vaccines for their workforce.’

What separates this camp from the Herd Immunity Guardian is where the decision sits, not whether requirements are legitimate. It has no quarrel with a facility that concludes masking and reassignment protect its patients adequately, and it does not ask legislatures to impose its judgment on employers who read the risk differently. That is why it fights in both directions: CMS itself withdrew the health care worker vaccination requirement in a 2023 final rule once the public health emergency ended, returning the choice to facilities, and where states have moved to take that choice away the hospital lobby has been the loudest objector. Even Arizona’s HCR 2056, the constitutional amendment approved by the state House in 2026 that would bar government and school vaccine requirements as a condition of employment or access to public facilities, carves out hospital districts to require health and safety protocols necessary to protect patients, a concession that concedes the camp’s premise.

The obvious objection is that a ward is not a classroom. A hospital selects its employees and can reassign them; a school district cannot pick its pupils, so an institution-decides rule leaves school-entry policy roughly where it found it. The harder objection comes from the other side: in a state with no employer mandate and no state requirement, a worker faces a rule set by a private party with no vote, no ballot box and no appeal short of quitting, which is precisely the coercion the Medical Freedom Campaigner names. This camp answers that a job in a nursing home is not a right to work there on any terms one likes, and that the resident down the hall has nowhere else to go.
positions.proponents: Infectious Diseases Society of America, Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America, Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society, American Hospital Association, Texas Hospital Association
positions.representative_note: Its July 2021 policy statement backed hospitals and health systems that choose, based on local factors, to require COVID-19 vaccination of their workforce; its state affiliates have fought bills that would take that choice away from the facility.

positions.name: Schedule Minimalist
positions.steelman: If it doesn’t spread across a classroom, it doesn’t belong on the school list.
positions.description: Compulsion has to be earned disease by disease, not issued as a package deal: the state may override a family’s no only where a disease spreads readily through ordinary classroom contact and is severe enough that an outbreak would be a genuine crisis. Measles and pertussis clear that bar easily. Hepatitis B, transmitted through blood and sexual contact, and chickenpox, mild in the overwhelming majority of healthy children, never should have been on the same list. Florida’s proposed 2026 rule, which would strike hepatitis B, varicella, Hib and pneumococcal shots from its school-entry list while leaving measles and pertussis requirements untouched, is the first serious test of drawing that line in statute.
positions.detail:
Hepatitis B’s school mandate has always been the odd one out. The CDC moved to universal infant vaccination in 1991 because the previous strategy of targeting risk groups had failed to bring cases down, most infected people having no identifiable risk factor at all, not because kindergartners were catching it from each other; states nonetheless folded it into school-entry law between 1994 and 1998. In 1999 the Association of American Physicians and Surgeons, through executive director Jane Orient, fought Ohio’s version of the mandate on exactly that ground: hepatitis B “is not spread by casual contact.”

The more careful version of the argument came from inside pediatrics itself. In a 2008 Pediatrics paper, Douglas Opel, Douglas Diekema and Edgar Marcuse critiqued the nine criteria Washington State used to decide which vaccines belong in a school immunization program and proposed adding a tenth: that a new mandate relate in some manner to increasing safety in the school environment. That criterion is the hinge this camp turns on, though its authors have not called for removing vaccines already on state lists, and Opel and Diekema have since urged caution about eliminating nonmedical exemptions, arguing the evidence is uncertain enough to warrant a more deliberative process. Chickenpox complicates the picture from the other direction: it does spread in classrooms, but pre-vaccine data put serious complications and deaths at a small fraction of cases among otherwise healthy children, so critics on the Herd Immunity Guardian side argue the minimalist test proves too much, since it would also drop Hib and pneumococcal, both respiratory-spread and both still capable of killing a young child. The camp’s reply: those series are completed in infancy, with the disease burden in children under two, so a kindergarten-entry requirement arrives years after the protection it is supposed to buy — on this camp’s test, exactly why they belong off the school list.

The argument has since moved from journals into statute books. Florida’s Department of Health approved a rule for public comment in August 2026 that would strike hepatitis B, varicella, Hib and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines from public and private school entry requirements, with final approval still pending, while state law continues to require MMR, polio and DTaP. The state’s own public rhetoric leaned more on parental authority than on the transmissibility test, which points to the position’s standing tension: winning the political fight has meant sharing a coalition with a broader medical-freedom push that would drop the whole schedule, not just the diseases that fail the classroom-spread test.
positions.proponents: Jane Orient / Association of American Physicians and Surgeons, Florida Department of Health and Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo (2026 proposed school-entry rule)
positions.representative_name: Association of American Physicians and Surgeons
positions.representative_note: Fought Ohio’s hepatitis B school mandate in 1999 on the ground that the disease “is not spread by casual contact”: the classroom-transmission test this camp applies vaccine by vaccine.

positions.name: Medical Freedom Campaigner
positions.steelman: If refusing costs a paycheck or a classroom seat, that is not consent. It is compliance.
positions.description: Consent to a medical procedure is not consent if refusing costs a job or a classroom seat: that is coercion wearing a lawful face. The right to control what enters one’s own body, or a minor child’s, sits prior to any public health calculus, because no third party can substitute its risk tolerance for another person’s. Every vaccine carries a nonzero chance of injury, and the federal government’s own compensation program has paid families over five billion dollars for vaccine injury since 1988, proof the risk is real enough that a no-fault federal court exists just to pay for it. When a harm, however rare, is severe enough to warrant a taxpayer-funded court, no employer or school board has standing to make refusing it cost a paycheck or an education.
positions.detail:
Mandates did not begin with COVID-19. Every U.S. state already required shots for school entry decades before 2020, and this camp’s grievance long predates the pandemic: the National Vaccine Information Center, founded in 1982 as Dissatisfied Parents Together after a wave of DPT-vaccine injury reports, has argued for over forty years that ‘informed consent’ cannot carry an asterisk for whichever diseases and shots a mandate happens to cover. The COVID-19 employer and school mandates of 2021 and 2022 turned that argument mainstream: New York City alone fired more than 1,400 municipal workers in February 2022 for declining the shot, and lawsuits invoking bodily autonomy, due process, and the federal Emergency Use Authorization statute’s consent-to-refuse language were filed by the hundreds nationwide. Most lost in court, but they built the movement’s current legal and political infrastructure, including Aaron Siri’s Informed Consent Action Network litigation and Children’s Health Defense’s Mandates Toolbox for state legislatures.

Internally, the camp divides over how far the principle reaches. A Del Bigtree wing treats it as near-absolute: no mandate for any vaccine, on the reasoning that parents will choose vaccination without coercion if a disease is truly severe enough to warrant it. A narrower wing, closer to NVIC’s own decades-old position, is willing to leave requirements on the books provided an unreviewed conscience or philosophical exemption always sits beside the medical one, blunting the mandate’s coercive edge without repealing it outright. What unites both wings is the Nuremberg Code’s opening line, ‘the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential,’ treated as the ethical floor beneath any vaccination policy, and the conviction that a government confident in a vaccine’s case should win it through persuasion and access, not through the threat of a lost job or a lost seat in class.
positions.proponents: National Vaccine Information Center (Barbara Loe Fisher), Children’s Health Defense (Mary Holland), Informed Consent Action Network (Aaron Siri, Del Bigtree)
positions.representative_note: The movement’s litigation engine, led by attorney Aaron Siri: suits over religious-exemption denials and informed-consent violations, open-records demands for vaccine safety data, and the Amish families’ challenge to New York’s repeal of its religious exemption.

positions.name: Vaccine Confidence Builder
positions.steelman: A mandate rents compliance; confidence buys coverage that stays.
positions.description: Confidence, not compulsion, is what moves a parent from ambivalence to the exam table, and the evidence is now trial-tested rather than intuition. Quebec’s PromoVac program trains maternity-ward nurses in motivational interviewing, a single postpartum conversation that respects a parent’s autonomy instead of overriding it, and it cut vaccine hesitancy by 40 percent and lifted infant coverage by seven percentage points at seven months, 75.9 percent against 68.6 percent. In the clinic the same logic holds: training pediatricians to presume the shot is happening rather than open the visit as a debate raised HPV vaccination rates by five points, a gain compulsion had nothing to do with. Build the access, the outreach and the trusted messenger, and coverage follows without the resentment a mandate leaves behind.
positions.detail:
Heidi Larson didn’t set out to build a philosophy of persuasion; she built the Vaccine Confidence Project in 2010 after watching a rumor collapse a polio campaign and realizing that coverage numbers alone told public health nothing about the trust underneath them. Her team’s global mapping work, and the WHO SAGE Working Group’s three Cs model of confidence, complacency and convenience, reframed hesitancy as a symptom of relationship rather than ignorance: people who distrust the institution offering a shot don’t need better facts, they need a better-trusted messenger.

Where the camp argues with itself is over how far outreach can carry the numbers on its own. Physician-led groups like Boost Oregon build their whole model around trust-based conversation, training clinicians and community health workers in motivational interviewing rather than leaning on any policy lever. Others, including parts of the CDC’s own Vaccinate with Confidence framework, launched in 2019 after that year’s measles outbreaks and later extended to COVID-19, run outreach alongside a mandate rather than instead of one, on the theory that access and trust-building are what make a requirement bearable, not a substitute for it. What unites them is a finding replicated across the PromoVac trials and Douglas Opel’s work on presumptive vaccine announcements: a single well-designed conversation moves coverage more than a scripted lecture does, without anyone needing to threaten a school seat.

The historical case against compulsion cuts the same way. Larson traces anti-vaccine sentiment back to the first smallpox vaccine at the close of the eighteenth century, and Britain’s anti-vaccination movement organized within a year of the 1853 Vaccination Act, which made infant smallpox vaccination compulsory, and the Anti-Compulsory Vaccination League followed in 1866: coercion has been generating its own opposition for two centuries. Building confidence instead is the one strategy in this fight that has never produced a backlash movement bearing its own name.
positions.proponents: Heidi Larson (Vaccine Confidence Project), Arnaud Gagneur (PromoVac/EMMIE program), Douglas Opel (presumptive vaccine communication research), WHO SAGE Working Group on Vaccine Hesitancy, Boost Oregon, CDC Vaccinate with Confidence framework
positions.representative_name: Heidi Larson / The Vaccine Confidence Project
positions.representative_note: Founded the Vaccine Confidence Project in 2010 and built its global Vaccine Confidence Index, arguing that hesitancy is a symptom of broken trust rather than of missing facts, and that a mandate cannot supply what trust supplies.

positions.name: Hassle Factor Architect
positions.steelman: Don’t abolish the exemption. Price it in effort, and a third of it goes away.
positions.description: Nonmedical exemptions should stay on the books, but getting one should take real effort: a counseling visit, an education module, a notarized form, an annual renewal. Michigan’s own data show why, since a rule effective in 2015 requiring parents to sit through waiver education at their local health department cut the statewide nonmedical exemption rate by roughly a third within a year, with counties new to the requirement dropping far more steeply than counties that already had one. Washington, Oregon and Vermont run variants of the same design: a practitioner’s signature, an online module, or reviewed educational material standing between a parent and the waiver. The point is not to punish conscience; it is to make sure the exemption reflects a considered choice rather than a default click, without touching the legal right to refuse.
positions.detail:
The fight over nonmedical exemptions has been framed as a binary: keep them as an unconditional right, or eliminate them the way a handful of states already have. Both options concede too much. Elimination may be right on the merits, but pushing for it now, amid falling trust in public health institutions and an emboldened anti-vaccine movement, risks losing the school mandate altogether — legislatures that would never vote to abolish the exemption outright may still be willing to make it harder to get. Michigan tested the alternative directly. A rule effective in 2015 required any parent seeking a nonmedical waiver to sit through an education session at their local health department before a school would accept it. In the year that followed, the statewide nonmedical exemption rate fell by roughly a third, and counties newly subject to the requirement saw far larger declines than the handful of counties that already had a version of it in place. Nobody’s right to refuse a vaccine was touched. What changed was how much it cost, in time and inconvenience, to exercise that right — and that alone did most of the work.

This is not a hypothetical policy; it is already the modal design in several states. Washington has required, since 2011, that the exemption form carry a health care practitioner’s signature attesting that the parent was given information on the risks and benefits of the vaccine, with a narrow carve-out for members of churches that reject medical treatment outright. Oregon gives parents a choice between that same practitioner signature and a certificate showing they completed an online educational module. Vermont asks parents claiming a religious exemption to review evidence-based educational material first. None of these states eliminated the exemption. All of them added a step between wanting one and having one, and the predicted mass flight from public schools never materialized.

The honest question inside this camp is how much friction is still just friction, and when it becomes elimination wearing a disguise. A fee, a workday-only counseling appointment for parents who cannot get childcare, or a form only a lawyer can complete correctly does not test conviction — it tests income and free time, and it will fall hardest on parents least equipped to navigate the system, not necessarily the most confident refusers. The people making this argument in print are the same ones who worry about it: Navin and Diekema’s own case against blanket elimination doubles as a case against burdens so heavy they function as elimination without saying so. A friction proponent has to be willing to say, of some specific proposed hurdle, that it goes too far — or the position collapses into the elimination stance it claims to be a moderate alternative to.
positions.proponents: Mark Navin, Mark Largent, Aaron McCright, Douglas Diekema
positions.representative_note: Philosophy, Oakland University and Corewell Health East; lead author of the Michigan waiver-education study and, with Diekema, of the JAMA Pediatrics case against eliminating exemptions.

crux.lead: Each camp names a bar compulsion must clear; one sets it where nothing clears it.
crux.lead_highlight: one sets it where nothing clears it
crux.subtitle: Severity, the coverage number, the sincerity of a belief, the trust spent buying compliance, whose institution carries the risk, the effort it takes to opt out, or the right to refuse at all: seven accounts of what a mandate must answer to.
crux.empirical: Then the states that tightened or loosened exemptions are the experiment, and the reading turns on the net: coverage gained, set against refusers who shift into homeschooling, private schools, or a broader exemption, and against whatever voluntary uptake slides years later. Trust leaves a measurable trace too, over a long enough window.
crux.values: Then no number reaches it. A mandate that raised coverage everywhere would still ask a person to accept a needle to keep a job or a classroom seat, and still ask a government to judge whose conviction counts as sincere. At stake is who carries an unchosen risk: the child who cannot be vaccinated, or the one vaccinated under compulsion.

actions.title: Support School Vaccine Requirements
actions.description: Vaccinate Your Family’s state advocacy hub helps residents contact legislators to oppose bills that would weaken school immunization requirements.

actions.title: Protect Vaccine Exemptions
actions.description: The National Vaccine Information Center tracks state exemption bills and organizes residents to push for protecting or expanding religious and personal-belief exemptions.

actions.title: Who Sets a Workplace Vaccine Rule
actions.description: The American Hospital Association’s policy statement sets out its case that the hospital or health system, judging local conditions, decides whether to require vaccination of its own workforce.

actions.title: Florida’s Vaccine Rule Rollback
actions.description: Florida’s Department of Health is taking public comment through mid-September 2026 on a rule dropping hepatitis B, chickenpox, Hib and pneumococcal from school-entry requirements.

actions.title: Become a Vax Ambassador
actions.description: Voices for Vaccines trains parent volunteers, its Vax Ambassadors, to talk with other families about vaccination in their communities without relying on mandates.

actions.title: Navin & Diekema, “Read the Room,” JAMA Pediatrics
actions.description: Navin and Diekema’s JAMA Pediatrics essay, the bioethicists’ own case for keeping nonmedical exemptions but pricing them in effort, published against the AAP’s call to eliminate them outright.

actions.title: Fund Vaccine Mandate Litigation
actions.description: Donations to the Informed Consent Action Network fund lawsuits challenging school, workplace and government vaccine mandates.

actions.title: Check Your State’s Requirements
actions.description: CDC’s state vaccination requirements page lets you look up the specific school, childcare and exemption rules in force where you live.

actions.title: School Vaccine Policy Explainer
actions.description: KFF’s explainer lays out which level of government sets school vaccine rules, current state requirements, and how exemption laws have shifted since 2025.
